m-01.title: Looking at the claim "Multiplying always makes it bigger"
m-01.goal: Learn that a few examples cannot guarantee "always," then build your own counterexamples where the product is not bigger than the starting number, and say when the product does get bigger.
m-01.material: Minji said, "Multiplying makes things bigger. 3×4=12 is bigger than 3, 5×2=10 is bigger than 5, and 7×6=42 is bigger than 7. So whatever number you multiply by, the result is always bigger than the number you started with!"
m-01.thinking.0: Checking whether a conclusion is overgeneralized even when there are many examples
m-01.thinking.2: Discovering the conditions under which a claim holds
m-01.prereq.0: Multiplying whole numbers by decimals (Grades 5-6 level, e.g. 8×0.5)
m-01.s.s1.prompt: Which line of Minji's argument is hard to believe? Pick one line.
m-01.s.s1.hint.0: First check whether each of the three calculations is correct.
m-01.s.s1.hint.1: Write down the numbers Minji multiplied by, 4, 2, and 6, side by side and see whether they have anything in common.
m-01.s.s1.line.3: So whatever number you multiply by, the result is always bigger than the number you started with.
m-01.s.s1.explain: What you see depends on which line you picked. If you picked one of the first three lines: those lines are correct in both the calculation and the comparison. The problem is not "Are the examples right?" but "How far can you go with just a few examples?" The last line is the wrong one. Minji looked at only three examples where the numbers multiplied by, 4, 2, and 6, are all the same kind of number, and then said "whatever number you multiply by, always." Even with many examples, if there is a kind of number you have not tested, "always" is not guaranteed.
m-01.s.s2.prompt: Make two examples with different multipliers that show Minji's claim is wrong. Use a whole number of 1 or more as the starting number and a number greater than 0 as the multiplier (a whole number or a decimal is fine), and the product must not be bigger than the starting number.
m-01.s.s2.hint.0: Minji only tested multipliers of 4, 2, and 6. Pick a kind of number that has not been tested yet and multiply it by the starting number.
m-01.s.s2.hint.1: Try changing the multiplier in different ways, compare each product with the starting number, and look for cases where it does not get bigger.
m-01.s.s2.ok.c1: The starting number is a whole number of 1 or more.
m-01.s.s2.fail.c1: Please use a whole number of 1 or more as the starting number.
m-01.s.s2.fail.c2: Please use a number greater than 0 as the multiplier. (0 is left out of this activity.)
m-01.s.s2.ok.c3: The product did not get bigger than the starting number. Minji's claim is broken.
m-01.s.s2.fail.c3: The product got bigger. Compare it with the starting number.
m-01.s.s2.explain: For example, 8×0.5=4 is smaller than 8, and 6×1=6 is equal to 6. Both are cases where it does "not get bigger." Even one counterexample is enough to break "always."
m-01.s.s3.prompt: When you multiply a starting number (a number greater than 0) by some number, which statement describes exactly, and without leaving anything out, when the result gets bigger than the starting number?
m-01.s.s3.hint.0: Change the multiplier in different ways and make a table of (starting number)×(multiplier).
m-01.s.s3.hint.1: In the table, separate the rows where the result is bigger than the starting number from the rows where it is not, and look at what is different about the multipliers.
m-01.s.s3.o.a: When the multiplier is greater than 1
m-01.s.s3.r.a: If the multiplier is greater than 1, the result gets bigger; if it is 1, it stays the same; if it is between 0 and 1, it gets smaller. This option states that boundary exactly.
m-01.s.s3.o.b: When the multiplier is a whole number
m-01.s.s3.r.b: Whole numbers include 1. Check what happens with 8×1 and you can fix this statement.
m-01.s.s3.o.c: When the multiplier is a decimal
m-01.s.s3.r.c: Some decimals, like 1.5, are greater than 1, and others, like 0.5, are smaller. Being a decimal alone does not decide it.
m-01.s.s3.o.d: When the multiplier is greater than 2
m-01.s.s3.r.d: If it is greater than 2, the result definitely gets bigger, but some numbers smaller than 2, like 1.5, also make it bigger. This does not cover every case where it gets bigger.
m-01.s.s3.o.e: When the starting number is big
m-01.s.s3.r.e: Even if the starting number is big, multiplying by 0.5 makes it smaller. The multiplier decides whether the result gets bigger.
m-01.s.s3.explain: If the multiplier is greater than 1, the result gets bigger; if it is 1, it stays the same; if it is between 0 and 1, it gets smaller. So the correct statement is not "It always gets bigger" but "Multiplying by a number greater than 1 makes it bigger."
m-01.s.s4.prompt: What would you like to tell Minji? Use the examples (numbers) you just made to write why she is wrong and when the result does get bigger.
m-01.s.s4.hint.0: You can use the numbers from the two examples you just made.
m-01.s.s4.hint.1: Start by saying "Minji, it doesn't work in cases like this," then add which numbers you have to multiply by to make it bigger.
m-01.s.s4.selfAssess.0: Is it clear that you compared the product with the starting number in your example?
m-01.s.s4.selfAssess.1: Did you know that even one example breaks "always"?
m-01.s.s4.selfAssess.2: Did you also say "which numbers make it bigger when you multiply"?
m-01.s.s4.model.0: No. 8×0.5=4 is smaller than 8. It only gets bigger than the starting number when the multiplier is greater than 1.
m-01.s.s4.model.1: It doesn't always get bigger. 6×1=6 stays the same, and 10×0.1=1 even got smaller. You have to multiply by a number greater than 1 to make it bigger.

m-02.title: What else do we need to solve this problem?
m-02.goal: Learn that whether a problem can be solved depends not on whether there are numbers but on whether the information needed for what you are asked to find is there, point out exactly what information is missing, and explain why the quotient has to be rounded up in a division with a remainder.
m-02.material:
Students going on a field trip want to split up into vans. There are four problems below.
a) 28 students split up and ride in vans. One van can carry at most 9 students. At least how many vans are needed?
b) 28 students go on a field trip. The entrance fee is 2000원 per student, and the van rental is 90000원 per van. What is the total entrance fee for all the students?
c) Students split up and ride in vans. One van can carry at most 9 students. At least how many vans are needed?
d) 28 students go on a field trip. One van can carry at most 9 students. How much does it cost in total to rent the vans?
m-02.thinking.0: Judging whether there is enough information
m-02.thinking.1: Telling needed information from unneeded information
m-02.thinking.2: Making several values that fit the conditions
m-02.prereq.0: Quotient and remainder in division (Grades 3-4 level)
m-02.s.s1.prompt: Read each problem separately and choose all the problems that can be answered using only the information in that problem.
m-02.s.s1.hint.0: In each of the four problems, underline what you are asked to find.
m-02.s.s1.hint.1: Write down which numbers you need to calculate what you are asked to find, and check one by one whether they are in the problem. Mark any numbers that are not used.
m-02.s.s1.r.a: If you missed problem a): it has both the 28 students and the capacity of 9 per van, so it can be solved.
m-02.s.s1.r.b: If you missed problem b): even though information that is not used in the solution, like the rental fee, is mixed in, you can find the "total entrance fee" you are asked for with 28×2000. Having extra information is different from missing information.
m-02.s.s1.r.c: If you chose problem c): even though numbers are given, there is information you absolutely need to find the answer. Check again which numbers you need to calculate what you are asked to find.
m-02.s.s1.r.d: If you chose problem d): you can find the number of vans (4), but to find the cost you need the rental fee for one van. This problem does not have that number.
m-02.s.s1.explain: Problem a) can be solved because it has the 28 students and the capacity of 9 per van. Problem b) does not use the rental fee, but it can be solved with "entrance fee × number of students" (2000×28=56000원). Problem c) does not say how many students there are, and problem d) does not give the rental fee for one van, so they cannot be solved. You can solve a problem even with unneeded information, but if the needed information is missing, you cannot solve it no matter how many numbers there are.
m-02.s.s2.prompt: What should you ask the teacher who wrote the problem so that you can solve problem c)?
m-02.s.s2.hint.0: Compare the numbers in problem c) and the numbers in problem a) side by side.
m-02.s.s2.hint.1: Find what information is in problem a) but not in problem c).
m-02.s.s2.o.a: How many students are there in total?
m-02.s.s2.r.a: Good question. The number of students is a number you absolutely need for what you are asked to find (the number of vans), and it is missing from the problem.
m-02.s.s2.r.b: How many vans are needed is what you are asked to find. Asking for what you are asked to find is not a question that gets you information.
m-02.s.s2.o.c: How many students can ride in one van?
m-02.s.s2.r.c: That information is already in problem c). Reread the problem and find which information is missing.
m-02.s.s2.o.d: How much is the rental fee per van?
m-02.s.s2.r.d: The rental fee is information that is used only after you know "how many vans." It is not used to find how many vans are needed.
m-02.s.s2.explain: Problem c) has the capacity per van but not the total number of students. You need both the total number of students and the capacity per van to find "how many vans."
m-02.s.s3.prompt: Pick a number of students so that exactly 3 vans are needed, and find three different numbers of students that work. (The capacity per van is 9.)
m-02.s.s3.hint.0: Find the most people that 2 vans can carry and the most people that 3 vans can carry.
m-02.s.s3.hint.1: Pick a number of students and count by hand how many vans are needed to carry them.
m-02.s.s3.ok.c1: The number of students is a whole number.
m-02.s.s3.fail.c1: Please use a whole number of 1 or more as the number of students.
m-02.s.s3.fail.c2: With this number of students, the number of vans is not 3. Check the most that 3 vans can carry and whether 2 vans are enough.
m-02.s.s3.explain: 2 vans can carry up to 18 students, and 3 vans can carry up to 27. So if there are 19 to 27 students (9 possibilities), exactly 3 vans are needed.
m-02.s.s4.prompt: With 27 students you need 3 vans, and with 28 students you need 4 vans. 28÷9=3.11…, so why 4 vans and not 3?
m-02.s.s4.hint.0: First write how many students can ride if all 3 vans are completely full.
m-02.s.s4.hint.1: Then compare that with 28 students and see whether anyone is left over.
m-02.s.s4.selfAssess.0: Does your explanation include the most that 3 vans can carry?
m-02.s.s4.selfAssess.1: Did you say that the leftover student also has to ride in a van?
m-02.s.s4.model.0: 3 vans can only carry up to 27 students, so 1 student is left over. That 1 student has to ride too, so one more van is needed, which makes 4 vans.
m-02.s.s4.model.1: If you put 28 students in 3 vans, only 27 can ride and 1 can't. So you need 4 vans. You can't just drop the part after the decimal point.
m-02.s.s4.model.2: 3 vans can't carry all 28 students. Even when full they carry 27, so one student is left over and we need one more van.
m-02.s.s4.model.3: 28 divided by 9 is 3 with 1 left over, but the leftover student has to ride too, so we need one more van.

m-03.title: Guessing what is inside the marble bag
m-03.goal: Change your first guess as more data comes in, and say why you should not be certain from the results of only a few draws.
m-03.material: A bag you can't see into has 10 marbles in total, red and blue. You take out one marble, look at its color, and put it back, and you do this many times. You don't know how many marbles there are of each color.
m-03.thinking.0: Changing your judgment when you see new data
m-03.thinking.1: Connecting the amount of data to how sure you are
m-03.thinking.2: Combining the results to choose the most reasonable explanation
m-03.prereq.0: Writing a part of a whole as a fraction or percentage (Grades 5-6 level)
m-03.prereq.1: Counting and organizing the counts in a table
m-03.s.s1.prompt: The data is revealed bit by bit. At each step, choose your idea about what is inside the bag.
m-03.s.s1.hint.0: At each step, divide the number of times red came out by the total number of draws to find the ratio.
m-03.s.s1.hint.1: For each option, divide the number of red marbles by 10 (the share of red in the bag) and compare it with the ratio in the data you drew.
m-03.s.s1.st.0.info: You drew 5 times and got red 4 times and blue 1 time.
m-03.s.s1.st.0.ask: Which color of marble do you think there are more of in the bag?
m-03.s.s1.st.0.after: Five draws is a small number, so there is a clue but it is not certain yet. It is right to say that red may be more.
m-03.s.s1.st.0.o.a: Red came out 4 times out of 5, so blue is due next, and there will be more blue
m-03.s.s1.st.0.r.a: The marble is put back, so the color that came out before does not change the next draw. Don't think in terms of "turns"; think in terms of how many times each color came out.
m-03.s.s1.st.0.o.b: Red came out 4 times, so there must be more red, and there is no need to draw any more
m-03.s.s1.st.0.r.b: Five draws is a small number. One color can come out a lot just by chance.
m-03.s.s1.st.0.o.c: Red may be more, but 5 draws is small and it could be chance, so we should draw more
m-03.s.s1.st.0.r.c: Good judgment. You thought about both things: there is a clue, but there are too few draws to be sure.
m-03.s.s1.st.0.o.d: Five draws tell us nothing about which color is more, so this result is useless
m-03.s.s1.st.0.r.d: It is not certain, but there is a clue. Red coming out more is also information.
m-03.s.s1.st.1.info: You increased it to 20 draws and got red 9 times and blue 11 times.
m-03.s.s1.st.1.after: With red 9 and blue 11 out of 20, the difference is not big. It is right to change your first guess and move toward thinking they are about the same.
m-03.s.s1.st.1.o.a: Red and blue came out about the same in 20 draws, so it is still hard to decide which one is more
m-03.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You judged using the newly collected data too. You corrected your first guess to fit the data.
m-03.s.s1.st.1.o.b: Red was more in the first 5 draws, so I think red is more, no matter the result of the 20 draws
m-03.s.s1.st.1.r.b: You are holding on to only the first 5 draws. What if you look at it together with the newly collected data?
m-03.s.s1.st.1.o.c: Blue came out 2 more times in 20 draws, so I am sure there is a lot more blue
m-03.s.s1.st.1.r.c: 9 and 11 are close. It is too early to be sure about "a lot more."
m-03.s.s1.st.2.info: You increased it to 50 draws and got red 19 times and blue 31 times.
m-03.s.s1.st.2.ask: Choose the number of marbles that best fits the ratio of red draws (19/50).
m-03.s.s1.st.2.after: The ratio of red draws, 19/50, is 0.38, which is closest to 0.4, the ratio for 4 marbles, among the options. 5 marbles (0.5) is not completely impossible, but it fits less well than 4. The more data you have, the narrower your guess gets.
m-03.s.s1.st.2.r.a: If there were 8 red, red would come out about 40 times in 50 draws. In reality it was 19 times.
m-03.s.s1.st.2.r.b: If there were 5, the ratio of red would be about 0.5, but the actual 19/50=0.38 is smaller than that. 5 is not completely impossible, but it is not the "best fit."
m-03.s.s1.st.2.r.c: 19/50=0.38 is closest to 0.4, the ratio for 4 marbles. You compared the ratios and chose the best fit.
m-03.s.s1.st.2.o.d: Any of them is equally likely
m-03.s.s1.st.2.r.d: When the data changes, how likely each one is changes too. Compare 19/50 with the ratio for each case.
m-03.s.s1.reflect: How were the results of the first 5 draws and the 50 draws different, and so how did you change your mind? How should your "certainty" be different when there is little data and when there is a lot of data?
m-03.s.s2.prompt: What would you like to tell a friend who shouted "There's more red!" after seeing only the first 5 draws?
m-03.s.s2.hint.0: Think about which result you would trust more, 5 draws or 50 draws, and write your reason.
m-03.s.s2.hint.1: End by suggesting to your friend what to try next.
m-03.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Which did you say: "there is little data" or "we should draw more"?
m-03.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you give the results of the 20 or 50 draws you saw as your reason?
m-03.s.s2.model.0: Five draws could just be chance, so let's draw more. When we did 20 and 50 draws, blue came out more.
m-03.s.s2.model.1: There are too few draws, so we're not sure yet. We need to do more.
m-03.s.s2.model.2: The sample is small, so we shouldn't be sure of the result. If we repeat it more times, it becomes more trustworthy.

m-04.title: Buying snacks with 5000원
m-04.goal: Find several ways to meet several conditions at the same time, and explain how to find them all without missing any and why some cases are impossible.
m-04.material: Our group of 10 people wants to buy snacks for a party. Chips cost 600원 per bag, jelly costs 400원 per bag, and drinks cost 500원 per bottle. We spend exactly 5000원, buy at least one of each of the three, and buy at least 10 items in total so that each person can have one.
m-04.thinking.1: Choosing a systematic way to search
m-04.thinking.2: Explaining impossible cases with even and odd numbers
m-04.prereq.0: Calculating amounts of money with multiplication and addition (Grades 3-4 level)
m-04.s.s1.prompt: Make three different purchase plans that meet all the conditions.
m-04.s.s1.hint.0: First decide how many of one kind to buy, then check whether you can buy the other two kinds with the remaining money.
m-04.s.s1.hint.1: If the total is short of or over 5000원, change the number of one kind by one at a time to fix the difference.
m-04.s.s1.fail.c1: You must buy at least one of each of the three kinds.
m-04.s.s1.fail.c2: Please use whole numbers for the counts.
m-04.s.s1.fail.c3: The total is not 5000원. Add up the amount for each kind to check.
m-04.s.s1.ok.c4: There are at least 10 items in total.
m-04.s.s1.fail.c4: There are fewer than 10 items in total, so each person cannot have one.
m-04.s.s1.explain: For example, (chips, jelly, drinks) = (4, 4, 2) is 2400+1600+1000=5000원 and 10 items. (3, 3, 4), (2, 2, 6), (1, 1, 8), (2, 7, 2), and (1, 6, 4) also all meet the conditions.
m-04.s.s2.prompt: After finding one way, you want to find the other ways without missing any. What is the best method?
m-04.s.s2.hint.0: Put the ways you found in a table and look at the order in which you found them.
m-04.s.s2.hint.1: For each option, compare "how far you search after finding one" and "whether you can tell you found them all."
m-04.s.s2.o.a: Set the number of bags of chips to 1, 2, 3... in order, and stop as soon as one way comes out
m-04.s.s2.r.a: Going in order is good. But if you stop after finding one, you can't tell whether there are more ways. You have to go as far as possible to find them all without missing any.
m-04.s.s2.o.b: Try calculations as they come to mind and keep only the ones that make 5000원, and stop when no more come out
m-04.s.s2.r.b: You can find a few ways. But you can't tell whether you "found them all." To find them all without missing any, you need an order.
m-04.s.s2.o.c: Set the number of bottles of drinks to 1, 2, 3... all the way through in order, and for each, check whether the rest can be bought with the remaining money
m-04.s.s2.r.c: A good method. If you fix one kind in order all the way through and check the rest, you can tell how far you have gone, so you can find them all without missing any.
m-04.s.s2.o.d: When the total is over 5000원, reduce all three kinds by one each and calculate again, and repeat
m-04.s.s2.r.d: The three kinds have different prices, so reducing them all equally does not fix the difference. It is easier to adjust by changing one kind at a time.
m-04.s.s2.explain: If you fix one kind in order, as far as possible, and check the rest, you can tell how far you have gone, so you can find them all without missing any. For example, you check by setting drinks to 1 bottle, 2 bottles, 3 bottles, and so on.
m-04.s.s3.prompt: Challenge (only if you want to try): In the ways you found, the number of drink bottles (500원) is 2, 4, 6, or 8, always even. Is there no way to buy an odd number of bottles of drinks (1, 3, 5...)? Explain in your own words why. Thinking about even and odd, units of 200원, or a table are all good.
m-04.s.s3.hint.0: Turn 600원, 400원, and 500원 into the number of 100원 bundles and write them as 6, 4, and 5.
m-04.s.s3.hint.1: Find the remaining money when you buy 1 bottle and 3 bottles of drinks, and check whether you can make that money with chips and jelly.
m-04.s.s3.placeholder: Example: The price of chips and jelly is ... If the number of drink bottles is odd, ...
m-04.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you write what is special about the amount you get by adding the prices of chips and jelly?
m-04.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you go on to write why the total can't be 5000원 when the number of drink bottles is odd?
m-04.s.s3.model.0: If you group 600원 and 400원 by 100원, you get 6 bundles and 4 bundles, both even. 5000원 is 50 bundles, which is even. A drink is 5 bundles, so with an odd number of bottles the sum is odd and can't be 50, which is even.
m-04.s.s3.model.1: Chips at 600원 and jelly at 400원 are both multiples of 200원, so their sum is also a multiple of 200. An odd number of bottles of drinks is 500, 1500, 2500..., and dividing by 200 leaves 100. So adding them can't make 5000원.
m-04.s.s3.model.2: With 1 bottle of drinks, the remaining money is 4500원, but any amount made with 600원 and 400원 is a multiple of 200, so 4500 can't be made. With 3 or 5 bottles, the remaining money is not a multiple of 200 either, so it doesn't work.

m-05.title: Which plan is cheaper?
m-05.goal: Tell apart what you can and cannot read as evidence from a table, and explain, using evidence, that in a linear function relationship which one is better depends on the condition (the amount used).
m-05.material:
There are two mobile data plans.
Plan A: base fee 9000원 + 1000원 per 1GB
Plan B: base fee 3000원 + 1500원 per 1GB

Monthly fee (원) by amount used
Amount used (GB) | Plan A fee | Plan B fee
0 | 9000 | 3000
4 | 13000 | 9000
8 | 17000 | 15000
12 | 21000 | 21000
16 | 25000 | 27000
20 | 29000 | 33000
m-05.thinking.1: Comparing and evaluating several claims using evidence
m-05.thinking.2: Reasoning about values that are not in the table using a rule
m-05.prereq.0: Equations and tables of linear functions (base fee + unit price form)
m-05.prereq.1: Reading and comparing values from a table
m-05.s.s1.prompt: Choose everything that you can read from the table.
m-05.s.s1.hint.0: In each row of the table, compare the fees of A and B and mark which one is smaller.
m-05.s.s1.hint.1: For each option, tell apart whether it talks only about amounts used that are in the table or goes on to values that are not in the table.
m-05.s.s1.o.a: At the amounts used in the table of 0, 4, and 8GB, B is cheaper.
m-05.s.s1.r.a: If you missed the 0, 4, and 8GB rows: in all three rows, the fee for B is smaller.
m-05.s.s1.o.b: At 12GB, the fees of the two plans are the same.
m-05.s.s1.r.b: If you missed the 12GB row: both A and B are 21000원. This is where the two fees switch places.
m-05.s.s1.o.c: At every amount used in the table, A is cheaper than B.
m-05.s.s1.r.c: Compare the two fees at 0GB. They start out different from the base fee.
m-05.s.s1.o.d: At 16GB and 20GB in the table, A is cheaper.
m-05.s.s1.r.d: If you missed the 16GB and 20GB rows: in both rows, the fee for A is smaller.
m-05.s.s1.o.e: Each time the amount used goes up by 4GB, the B fee goes up by 4000원.
m-05.s.s1.r.e: Calculate yourself the difference between the B fees at 0GB and 4GB. If it is 1500원 per 1GB, how much is 4GB?
m-05.s.s1.explain: At 0, 4, and 8GB B is cheaper (3000<9000, 9000<13000, 15000<17000), at 12GB they are the same (21000), and at 16GB and 20GB A is cheaper (25000<27000, 29000<33000). B goes up by 6000원 for every 4GB.
m-05.s.s2.prompt: Three friends said which plan is cheaper. Considering both the table and the fee rules, which claim is the most appropriate?
m-05.s.s2.hint.0: Find in the table where the fees of A and B switch places.
m-05.s.s2.hint.1: Write down which one is cheaper before and after the switch.
m-05.s.s2.o.a: Jisu: A is cheaper, because its fee per 1GB is 1000원, which is less than B's 1500원.
m-05.s.s2.r.a: Look again at 0GB, 4GB, and 8GB in the table. Even though the unit price is lower, what happens at first because of the base fee?
m-05.s.s2.o.b: Minho: B is cheaper, because its base fee is 3000원, which is cheaper than A's 9000원.
m-05.s.s2.r.b: Look again at 16GB and 20GB in the table. As the amount used goes up, what happens to the difference in the base fee?
m-05.s.s2.o.c: Hana: It depends on the amount used. Below 12GB, B is cheaper; above it, A is cheaper.
m-05.s.s2.r.c: This judgment is right for both the table and the fee rules. The base fee and the unit price go in opposite directions, so they switch at 12GB.
m-05.s.s2.o.d: Junho: It's the same whichever you pick, because at 12GB the fee is the same, 21000원.
m-05.s.s2.r.d: In the table, 12GB is the only amount used where the fees are the same. Look at the other rows again.
m-05.s.s2.o.e: Seoa: It depends on the amount used. Below 8GB, B is cheaper; above it, A is cheaper.
m-05.s.s2.r.e: At 8GB, B is still cheaper (15000원 and 17000원). The place where the two fees become equal and switch is 12GB, not 8GB.
m-05.s.s2.explain: B's base fee is 6000원 cheaper, and A's unit price is 500원 cheaper. They meet at 12GB; below that B is cheaper, and above that A is cheaper. If you look at only one amount used, you can overgeneralize wrongly like Jisu or Minho.
m-05.s.s3.prompt: Which plan would you recommend to someone who uses 10GB a month? 10GB is not in the table. Write what you based your judgment on.
m-05.s.s3.hint.0: Look again at which one is cheaper in the 8GB and 12GB rows, and think about the fact that 10GB is between them.
m-05.s.s3.hint.1: Use the fee rules (base fee and fee per 1GB) to calculate both fees at 10GB yourself.
m-05.s.s3.selfAssess.0: For 10GB, which is not in the table, what did you base your answer on (calculating with the formula, or being between 8GB and 12GB)?
m-05.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you know you were assuming that the fee goes up at a steady rate?

m-06.title: Checking Seoyeon's solution
m-06.goal: Learn that dividing both sides of an equation by an expression with a variable can lose a solution if you miss the possibility that it is 0, fix the solution, and make an equation where the same thing happens.
m-06.material: Seoyeon solved the equation x² (x squared) = 3x like this. Look at the solution one line at a time and check whether it is correct.
m-06.thinking.0: Finding where and why the error is in a solution
m-06.thinking.1: Fixing the error and finishing the solution
m-06.thinking.2: Making a case where the same error happens
m-06.prereq.0: Solving quadratic equations by factoring (Grade 9 level)
m-06.prereq.1: Checking the solution of an equation by substituting
m-06.s.s1.prompt: Pick one line in this solution that you can't trust. (You can pick a line with a wrong step, or a line where a wrong conclusion is written because of it.)
m-06.s.s1.hint.0: Check one line at a time whether each line follows properly from the line right before it.
m-06.s.s1.hint.1: Try putting x = 0 into the original equation x² = 3x and see whether it holds.
m-06.s.s1.line.1: Divide both sides by x to get x = 3
m-06.s.s1.line.2: Substituting x = 3 gives 3² = 9 and 3×3 = 9, so it holds.
m-06.s.s1.line.3: So the only solution of this equation is x = 3.
m-06.s.s1.explain: What you see depends on which line you picked. If you picked the 3rd line (substitution): that line is a correct calculation. But substitution only shows that "3 is a solution"; it does not show that "there are no other solutions." If you picked the 1st line: it is the original equation, so there is no problem. The wrong places are the 2nd line and the 4th line. In the 2nd line, both sides were divided by x, but x might be 0, and you cannot divide by 0. So the solution x = 0 disappeared, and as a result the wrong conclusion in the 4th line, "the only solution is 3," came out.
m-06.s.s2.prompt: Find all the solutions of x² = 3x correctly, and explain where Seoyeon's solution went wrong.
m-06.s.s2.hint.0: Write what form you get when you move all the terms to one side and factor.
m-06.s.s2.hint.1: Put Seoyeon's solution and your solution side by side and find the point where the solutions become different.
m-06.s.s2.placeholder: Example: If I move the terms and simplify, ...
m-06.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you check by putting x = 0 and x = 3 into the original equation?
m-06.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Does your explanation include the point that "when you divide both sides by an expression, you must first check that the expression is not 0"?
m-06.s.s2.model.0: x²−3x=0, x(x−3)=0, so x=0 or x=3. When dividing both sides by x, x could be 0, and you can't divide by 0, so I missed the solution x=0.
m-06.s.s2.model.1: There are two solutions, 0 and 3. x=0 also holds when put into the original equation, 0=0, but when both sides were divided by x, the case x=0 disappeared.
m-06.s.s3.prompt: Make two different quadratic equations ax² + bx + c = 0 where the same thing happens as with Seoyeon. Conditions: it is a quadratic equation, dividing both sides by x makes you miss the solution x = 0, and the other solution must not be 0. (a, b, and c are integers.)
m-06.s.s3.hint.0: Write which terms are left when you put x = 0 into ax² + bx + c = 0.
m-06.s.s3.hint.1: Compare with the form you get by moving Seoyeon's equation x² = 3x to one side, and match the values of a, b, and c.
m-06.s.s3.ok.c1: It is a quadratic equation and the coefficients are integers.
m-06.s.s3.fail.c1: a must be an integer that is not 0, and b and c must also be integers.
m-06.s.s3.ok.c2: The equation holds even when you substitute x = 0. So dividing by x makes you miss the solution 0.
m-06.s.s3.fail.c2: Substitute x = 0. Does the equation hold? If it does not hold, 0 is not a solution, so there is no solution to miss.
m-06.s.s3.fail.c3: If b is 0, the only solution is 0. Change it into an equation whose other solution is not 0.
m-06.s.s3.explain: For x = 0 to be a solution, only the constant term c is left when you put 0 in for x, so c = 0 is needed. For example, x² − 3x = 0 and 2x² − 4x = 0 both lose the solution 0 if you divide by x. For equations like these, it is safe to solve by factoring out x as a common factor.

m-07.title: If the averages are the same, are the classes the same?
m-07.goal: Show with data you make yourself that the spread of the data can differ even when the averages are the same, and use this to make a question for a friend to solve.
m-07.material: Three students were picked from each of Class 1 and Class 2 and their math scores were checked, and the average for both classes was 70 points. The teacher said, "Since the averages are the same, we can say the scores of the two classes are similar." (The students picked are imaginary students.)
m-07.thinking.0: Judging the limits of comparing using only the average
m-07.thinking.1: Making data yourself to fit conditions
m-07.thinking.2: Making a question whose answer is decided by the data
m-07.prereq.1: Difference between the maximum and minimum (range)
m-07.s.s1.prompt: Which is the most appropriate thought about the teacher's statement?
m-07.s.s1.hint.0: Think of one set of three scores whose average is 70.
m-07.s.s1.hint.1: Make two different sets of three scores with an average of 70 and compare them.
m-07.s.s1.o.a: If the averages are the same, the scores will generally be gathered to a similar degree
m-07.s.s1.r.a: The average sums up the values as one number, so it does not tell you whether the scores are gathered or spread out. Compare the case where all three scores are the same with the case where they are far apart.
m-07.s.s1.o.b: Even if the averages are the same, how spread out the scores are can be different in the two classes
m-07.s.s1.r.b: You pointed out that even when the averages are the same, the scores can be gathered or far apart.
m-07.s.s1.o.c: If the averages are the same, the highest scores will generally be similar too
m-07.s.s1.r.c: Even with the same average, one class may have all similar scores and the other may have a mix of high and low scores. You can't say the top scores are the same.
m-07.s.s1.explain: Even with the same average, the scores can be gathered like 70, 70, 70 or spread out like 40, 70, 100. Let's make them and check in the next step.
m-07.s.s2.prompt: Make scores (whole numbers from 0 to 100) for the two classes. Conditions: each class has an average of 70 points, and Class 2's (highest score − lowest score) must be at least 20 points bigger than Class 1's. Changing only the order of the scores counts as the same example, so make two different combinations of scores.
m-07.s.s2.hint.0: First choose three scores for Class 1 that add up to 210, and calculate the difference between the highest and lowest scores.
m-07.s.s2.hint.1: For Class 2, keep the sum at 210 and try raising one score and lowering another to see whether you can make the difference bigger.
m-07.s.s2.fail.c1: Scores must be at least 0 and at most 100.
m-07.s.s2.fail.c2: Please use whole numbers for the scores.
m-07.s.s2.fail.c3: The sum of Class 1's three scores is not 210. The sum must be 210 for the average to be 70 points.
m-07.s.s2.fail.c4: The sum of Class 2's three scores is not 210.
m-07.s.s2.ok.c5: Class 2 is more spread out than Class 1 by at least 20 points.
m-07.s.s2.fail.c5: Class 2's (highest score − lowest score) is not at least 20 points bigger than Class 1's. Calculate the difference for each class and compare them.
m-07.s.s2.explain: Both classes have an average of 70 points, but for 70, 70, 70 the difference is 0 points and for 40, 70, 100 it is 60 points. Even with the same average, how spread out the scores are can be different.
m-07.s.s3.prompt: Using the scores of the two classes you just made, make one question a friend can solve, and write the answer too. (Example: "Which class has the higher ○○?")
m-07.s.s3.hint.0: Pick one different value from the two classes' highest score, lowest score, and difference, and turn it into a question.
m-07.s.s3.hint.1: After writing the question, look at your scores as they are and say the answer. Check that there is only one answer.
m-07.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Is the answer decided by only the scores of the two classes you made?
m-07.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Is this a question that can't be answered just from the fact that "the averages are the same"?
m-07.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Would another friend get the same answer using your data?
m-07.s.s3.model.0: Question: Of Class 1 (70, 70, 70) and Class 2 (40, 70, 100), which class has scores that are more evenly gathered? Answer: Class 1. The difference between the highest and lowest scores is 0 points, which is smaller than Class 2's 60 points.
m-07.s.s3.model.1: Question: Both classes have an average of 70 points, so which class has the higher top score? The answer is Class 2 (100 points). Even with the same average, the top score can be different.

m-08.title: Find all the triangles with perimeter 12
m-08.goal: Discover by testing the condition for a triangle to be formed, and explain how you can be sure you have systematically found all the cases that meet the condition.
m-08.material: There are several sticks. You want to pick three sticks and use them as sides to make a triangle. The lengths of the sticks are all whole numbers (cm), and the perimeter, the sum of the three lengths, is 12cm. You don't cut them or join them together.
m-08.thinking.0: Testing a hypothesis yourself to discover the condition for it to hold
m-08.thinking.1: Finding all the cases within constraints
m-08.thinking.2: Explaining the reason you found them all without missing any
m-08.prereq.0: Sides and perimeter of a triangle
m-08.prereq.1: Basics of inequalities (comparing the sum of two numbers with one number)
m-08.s.s1.prompt: Can you make a triangle from three sticks of 3cm, 3cm, and 6cm? (The sum is 12cm.) Judge it by imagining that you lay them out yourself.
m-08.s.s1.hint.0: Lay the longest stick, 6cm, on the ground, and stand the other two sticks up at both ends so that they touch.
m-08.s.s1.hint.1: Add the lengths of the other two sticks and compare with the longest stick.
m-08.s.s1.r.a: 3+3+6=12, so the perimeter is right. But having the right perimeter is different from the triangle closing. What happens when you put the two sticks against the 6cm stick?
m-08.s.s1.r.b: Good judgment. Even if you join two 3cm sticks above the 6cm stick, the length is the same, so no top vertex is formed.
m-08.s.s1.o.c: You can't know until you draw it yourself.
m-08.s.s1.r.c: You can think about it by comparing the lengths of the sticks, without drawing it. Which lengths should you compare?
m-08.s.s1.explain: Even if you join two 3cm sticks, the length is 6cm, the same as the 6cm stick. The two sticks lie flat on top of the 6cm stick and no vertex is formed, so it doesn't make a triangle.
m-08.s.s2.prompt: Find and enter all the different triangles with a perimeter of 12cm where all the side lengths are whole numbers. (Triangles whose sides are only in a different order count as the same triangle.)
m-08.s.s2.hint.0: First decide the length of the longest side, then find the sum of the other two sides that goes with it.
m-08.s.s2.hint.1: Check whether the three sides you made form a triangle by comparing the longest side with the sum of the other two sides.
m-08.s.s2.ok.c1: The three side lengths are whole numbers.
m-08.s.s2.fail.c1: Please use whole numbers of 1 or more for the side lengths.
m-08.s.s2.fail.c2: The sum of the three sides is not 12.
m-08.s.s2.fail.c3: A triangle is not formed. Compare the longest side with the sum of the other two sides.
m-08.s.s2.explain: The only triangles that meet the conditions are (2, 5, 5), (3, 4, 5), and (4, 4, 4). If the longest side is equal to or greater than the sum of the other two sides, like (3, 3, 6) or (1, 5, 6), no triangle is formed.
m-08.s.s3.prompt: How can you be sure that "this is all, there are no more"? Explain the method you used to find them all without missing any.
m-08.s.s3.hint.0: First find the largest and smallest lengths the longest side can be.
m-08.s.s3.hint.1: Once the longest side is decided, write what the sum of the other two sides is and check each possible pair one by one.
m-08.s.s3.placeholder: Example: If the longest side is ...
m-08.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you clearly write what criterion (such as the longest side) you used to split into cases?
m-08.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you check with numbers which are possible and which are impossible in each case?
m-08.s.s3.model.0: The longest side must be less than 6, so it is 5 or less, and it is at least 12÷3=4. If the longest side is 4, there is only 4,4,4. If it is 5, the sum of the other two is 7, so there are two ways: (2,5) and (3,4). So there are three in all.
m-08.s.s3.model.1: I checked in order from when the shortest side is 1 to when it is 4. If it is 1, the sum of the other two is 11, and all of them like 5,6 don't make a triangle; if it is 2, 5,5; if it is 3, 4,5; if it is 4, 4,4. Checking one by one like this, nothing is missed.
m-08.s.s3.model.2: I fixed one side and split up the remaining sum. If the longest side is 5, the sum of the other two is 7, so (2,5) and (3,4); if it is 4, only (4,4). I checked every case this way, so there are 3.

m-09.title: It tested positive. What is the probability it is defective?
m-09.goal: Change your judgment about the probability of being defective each time a new test result comes in, and explain why you overestimate the probability if you ignore the original defect rate (the prior probability).
m-09.material: 2% of the products made at a factory are defective. The tester marks a defective product as "positive" (a mark meaning defective) with a 90% probability, and it also wrongly marks a normal product as "positive" with a 5% probability. A mark meaning not defective is "negative." When it is already decided whether a product is defective or normal, assume that even if you test that product many times, the results of the tests do not affect each other.
m-09.thinking.0: Revising a probability judgment as more information comes in
m-09.thinking.1: Comparing intuition and calculation for conditional probability
m-09.thinking.2: Explaining the effect of the base rate (defect rate)
m-09.prereq.1: Meaning of conditional probability (Probability and Statistics level)
m-09.s.s1.prompt: The test results are revealed one at a time. Each time, choose about how likely it is that the product is defective.
m-09.s.s1.hint.0: Suppose there are 1000 products, and first write how many are defective and how many are normal.
m-09.s.s1.hint.1: Count how many defective products and how many normal products give the result in question (positive, two positives, and so on).
m-09.s.s1.st.0.info: One product was tested and came out "positive."
m-09.s.s1.st.0.ask: About what is the probability that this product is defective?
m-09.s.s1.st.0.after: Out of 1000, 20 are defective and 980 are normal. Of the 20 defective, 90%, which is 18, are positive, and of the 980 normal, 5%, which is 49, are also positive. Of the 67 positives, 18 are truly defective, so it is about 27%. There are far more normal products, so even if the tester is fairly accurate, the probability comes out low.
m-09.s.s1.st.0.r.a: The defect rate is 2%, so it looks low, but the information that the result was positive raises the probability.
m-09.s.s1.st.0.r.b: Of the 67 positives out of 1000, 18 are defective, which matches the value you counted.
m-09.s.s1.st.0.r.c: 90% is "the probability that a defective product is positive." "The probability that a positive product is defective" is a different value. Think about the fact that there are far more normal products.
m-09.s.s1.st.0.r.d: It feels high because of the tester's accuracy. Suppose there are 1000 products in total and count how many positives come out.
m-09.s.s1.st.1.info: The same product was tested once more, and it is "positive" again.
m-09.s.s1.st.1.ask: Now about what is the probability that it is defective?
m-09.s.s1.st.1.after: Of the 20 defective out of 1000, 0.9×0.9=0.81, that is 16.2, are positive twice, and of the 980 normal, 0.05×0.05=0.0025, that is 2.45, are positive twice. 16.2÷(16.2+2.45)≈0.87, so it is about 87%. One positive is weak, but positives in a row raise the probability a lot.
m-09.s.s1.st.1.r.a: A normal product can also be positive twice in a row (0.05×0.05). Look at how many that is.
m-09.s.s1.st.1.r.b: The second positive is new information. If you count only the cases that are positive twice in a row, how does the share of defective products change?
m-09.s.s1.st.1.r.c: It went up from the first 27%, but it may go up by more. Count by hand only the cases that are positive both times.
m-09.s.s1.st.1.r.d: This matches the value you got by counting the cases positive both times (about 87%).
m-09.s.s1.st.2.info: The third test came out "negative." (The first two were positive.)
m-09.s.s1.st.2.ask: Now about what is the probability that it is defective?
m-09.s.s1.st.2.after: Of the 20 defective, positive-positive-negative is 0.9×0.9×0.1=0.081, that is 1.62, and of the 980 normal, positive-positive-negative is 0.05×0.05×0.95=0.002375, that is 2.3275. 1.62÷(1.62+2.3275)≈0.41, so it is about 41%. New information can raise or lower the probability.
m-09.s.s1.st.2.r.a: This matches the value you got by comparing about 1.62 defective and about 2.33 normal products that give positive-positive-negative (about 41%).
m-09.s.s1.st.2.r.b: The third negative is information that lowers the chance of being defective. What is the probability that a defective product is negative?
m-09.s.s1.st.2.r.c: Even though one negative came out, the first two positives don't disappear. What happens when you take all three results into account?
m-09.s.s1.st.2.r.d: Looking at the third negative alone, it seems like it should go down, but there are already two positives before it. Count the cases that give positive-positive-negative on the defective side and on the normal side, and compare them.
m-09.s.s1.reflect: Over the three tests, the probability of being defective changed from 27% to 87% to 41%. In which direction, and why, did each test result move the probability? What did your first intuition of 90% leave out?
m-09.s.s2.prompt: Explain to a friend who believes "The tester catches 90% of defective products, so if it's positive, it's 90% or more likely to be defective" why that is not so.
m-09.s.s2.hint.0: Out of 1000 products, split the products that come out positive into defective and normal and count them.
m-09.s.s2.hint.1: Among those positive products, calculate the share that are truly defective.
m-09.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you tell apart "the probability that a defective product is positive" from "the probability that a positive product is defective" in your explanation?
m-09.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you mention the number of normal products that come out positive?
m-09.s.s2.model.0: Defective products are only 2% to begin with, so that is 20 out of 1000. Of the 980 normal ones, 5%, which is 49, also come out positive. Of the 67 positives, 18 are truly defective, so it is about 27%.
m-09.s.s2.model.1: Even if the tester is 90%, there are far more normal products, so there are more products that are normal but positive than products that are defective and positive. So one positive does not make it 90%.
m-09.s.s2.model.2: Defective products are very rare and most products are normal, so the number of products wrongly marked positive even though they are normal can be larger than the number of truly defective positives. So even if it is positive, the chance of being defective is not high.

m-10.title: If f'(a)=0, is it an extremum?
m-10.goal: Use data on the sign changes of the derivative as evidence to judge the claim "If f'(a)=0, it is an extremum," build a counterexample, and state the condition for it to be an extremum.
m-10.material:
Jihun said, "For a function f, if f'(a)=0, then it has an extremum (a maximum or minimum) at x=a." He checked the sign of the derivative f'(x) of three functions near x=0.
Function | f'(x) | f'(−1) | f'(−0.1) | f'(0) | f'(0.1) | f'(1)
f(x)=x² | 2x | − | − | 0 | + | +
f(x)=x³ | 3x² | + | + | 0 | + | +
f(x)=−x⁴ | −4x³ | + | + | 0 | − | −
(The + and − in the table are the signs of the derivative values. Read x², x³, and −x⁴ as "x squared," "x cubed," and "negative x to the fourth.")
m-10.thinking.0: Judging a claim with evidence from a table
m-10.thinking.2: Discovering the condition for it to hold
m-10.prereq.1: Sign of the derivative, increasing and decreasing, meaning of maximum and minimum (Calculus level)
m-10.s.s1.prompt: Look at the table and choose all the functions that you judge to have an extremum (a maximum or minimum) at x=0.
m-10.s.s1.hint.0: For each function, compare the signs of f' to the left and right of x=0.
m-10.s.s1.hint.1: Use the fact that when the sign changes, the function changes from increasing to decreasing (or the other way around).
m-10.s.s1.r.a: If you missed x²: the sign of f' changes from − to +. It is where the function goes from decreasing to increasing, so it is a minimum.
m-10.s.s1.r.b: The sign of f'(x) is + both before and after x=0. It increases, stops for a moment at 0, and then increases again, so it is not an extremum.
m-10.s.s1.r.c: If you missed −x⁴: the sign of f' changes from + to −. It is where the function goes from increasing to decreasing, so it is a maximum.
m-10.s.s1.explain: For x², the sign of f' changes from − to +, so it is a minimum, and for −x⁴, it changes from + to −, so it is a maximum. For x³, f'(0)=0 but the sign does not change, so it is not an extremum.
m-10.s.s2.prompt: Which is the most appropriate judgment about Jihun's claim "If f'(a)=0, then there is an extremum at x=a"?
m-10.s.s2.hint.0: If a claim says "always," think about what makes it false when there is even one case.
m-10.s.s2.hint.1: For each function in the table, compare the signs of f' before and after x=0 when f'(0)=0.
m-10.s.s2.o.a: It is true. All three functions in the table have f'(0)=0, so they have an extremum.
m-10.s.s2.r.a: All three functions have f'(0)=0, but only two of them have an extremum. Check all the results in the table.
m-10.s.s2.o.b: It is false. Even if f'(0)=0, there is a function in the table that does not have an extremum.
m-10.s.s2.r.b: You showed with one counterexample that "always" is false.
m-10.s.s2.o.c: It is true. Two of the three functions in the table have an extremum, so it holds for most of them.
m-10.s.s2.r.c: A claim that says "always" does not become true because it holds for most cases. Look for whether there is even one case where it does not hold.
m-10.s.s2.o.d: It cannot be judged. There are only three functions in the table, so it is hard to decide.
m-10.s.s2.r.d: Even with few functions, if there is one counterexample, you can judge "always" to be false. Look for whether the counterexample is in the table.
m-10.s.s2.explain: f(x)=x³ has f'(0)=0 but is not an extremum, so it is a counterexample. The claim that "it always holds" becomes false with just one counterexample.
m-10.s.s3.prompt: Make two cubic functions f(x)=ax³+bx²+cx+d (integer coefficients) with different values of a, where f'(0)=0 but there is no extremum at x=0.
m-10.s.s3.hint.0: Write f'(x) in terms of a, b, and c, and find f'(0).
m-10.s.s3.hint.1: Compare why x³ in the table was not an extremum (the sign of f') and how it differs from x².
m-10.s.s3.ok.c1: It is a cubic function and the coefficients are integers.
m-10.s.s3.fail.c1: a must be an integer that is not 0, and b, c, and d must also be integers.
m-10.s.s3.fail.c2: f'(0) is not 0. Put x=0 into f'(x)=3ax²+2bx+c.
m-10.s.s3.ok.c3: f'(x)=3ax², so the sign does not change before and after x=0.
m-10.s.s3.fail.c3: The sign of f'(x) changes before and after x=0, so an extremum forms. Look at the sign near x=0 in f'(x)=x(3ax+2b).
m-10.s.s3.explain: f'(x)=3ax²+2bx+c, so f'(0)=c. If c=0, then f'(x)=x(3ax+2b), and if b≠0, the sign changes near x=0 and an extremum forms. If b=0, then f'(x)=3ax², so the sign is the same before and after x=0 and it is not an extremum.
m-10.s.s4.prompt: You want to correct Jihun's claim properly. In "If f'(a)=0 and ______, then it has an extremum at x=a," write the condition that goes in the blank.
m-10.s.s4.hint.0: For x² and −x⁴ (the cases that are extrema) and x³ (the case that is not), compare how the sign of f' differs before and after x=0.
m-10.s.s4.hint.1: Write side by side the signs to the left and right of x=0 for x² and x³, and write in one sentence what is different.
m-10.s.s4.selfAssess.0: Did you write it as a condition that compares the left and right of x=a?
m-10.s.s4.selfAssess.1: Does the condition rule out the case of x³, where f'(x)=0 at x=0 but it is not an extremum?
m-10.s.s4.model.0: The sign of f'(x) changes before and after x=a.
m-10.s.s4.model.1: It is the case where, to the left of x=a, it is increasing and then to the right it changes to decreasing (or the reverse), that is, where increasing and decreasing switch.
m-10.s.s4.model.2: On the left and right of x=a, f'(x) changes from + to − or from − to +.
m-10.s.s4.model.3: f''(a)≠0. (If the second derivative is not 0, it is an extremum.)
m-10.s.s4.modelNote.3: This is the second derivative test. It is a sufficient condition but not a necessary condition.

m-11.title: What do we need to know to determine a quadratic function?
m-11.goal: Judge which sets of information determine a quadratic function uniquely, and, for the sets with too little information, show two different functions that meet the conditions yourself to decide what extra information is needed.
m-11.material: You want to find the equation of the quadratic function f(x)=ax²+bx+c (a≠0). Among the sets of information below, you want to find the ones where that information alone determines the equation uniquely.
m-11.thinking.0: Judging whether there is enough information
m-11.thinking.1: Showing that information is not enough with two different examples
m-11.prereq.0: Three forms of a quadratic function (standard form, vertex form, factored form)
m-11.prereq.2: Substituting points the graph passes through
m-11.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the sets where that information alone determines the quadratic function uniquely.
m-11.s.s1.hint.0: In f(x)=ax²+bx+c, first count how many unknowns you need to find.
m-11.s.s1.hint.1: Check how many different equations (conditions) each option gives, and whether those conditions determine all of a, b, and c.
m-11.s.s1.o.a: The vertex, and one point on the graph that is not the vertex
m-11.s.s1.r.a: If it is the vertex, p and q are determined in f(x)=a(x−p)²+q, and one point determines a.
m-11.s.s1.o.b: Two different points on the graph, and the fact that the graph opens upward
m-11.s.s1.r.b: There are infinitely many upward-opening parabolas through two points. The direction it opens tells you only the sign of a, not the value of a.
m-11.s.s1.o.c: Two points where it meets the x-axis, and the x-coordinate of the vertex
m-11.s.s1.r.c: The x-coordinate of the vertex is exactly halfway between the two x-intercepts, so it is not new information. a is still left over. Try multiplying (x−1)(x−3) by 2 or −5.
m-11.s.s1.o.d: Three points on the graph with different x-coordinates
m-11.s.s1.r.d: Three points give three independent equations in a, b, and c, so it is determined uniquely.
m-11.s.s1.o.e: The equation of the axis of symmetry and the y-intercept
m-11.s.s1.r.e: The axis of symmetry fixes one relationship between a and b, and the y-intercept fixes c. Count whether all three values a, b, and c are determined.
m-11.s.s1.o.f: Two points where it meets the x-axis, and one other point on the graph
m-11.s.s1.r.f: In f(x)=a(x−p)(x−q), p and q are determined, and one point determines a.
m-11.s.s1.explain: There are three unknowns, a, b, and c, so you need three independent conditions. D: three points give three simultaneous equations. A: the vertex determines p and q in f(x)=a(x−p)²+q, and one point determines a. F: p and q are determined in f(x)=a(x−p)(x−q), and one point determines a. B, C, and E have only two independent conditions, so a is left over. (If three points are on a straight line, no quadratic function exists, so under the condition that it is a quadratic function, the three points are not on a straight line.)
m-11.s.s2.prompt: You want to show that the information in option E, "the y-intercept is 1 and the axis of symmetry is x=2," does not determine the equation by itself. Make two different quadratic functions f(x)=ax²+bx+c that meet both of these conditions.
m-11.s.s2.hint.0: The axis of symmetry is x=−b/(2a), so write the relationship between a and b that makes this equal to 2.
m-11.s.s2.hint.1: Decide a first, then fit b and c to the conditions. Check that the conditions still hold when you change a.
m-11.s.s2.ok.c1: Since a is not 0, it is a quadratic function.
m-11.s.s2.fail.c1: a must not be 0 for it to be a quadratic function.
m-11.s.s2.ok.c2: The y-intercept (the value when x=0) is 1.
m-11.s.s2.fail.c2: The y-intercept is the value you get by putting in x=0, f(0)=c. This is not 1.
m-11.s.s2.ok.c3: The axis of symmetry is x=2.
m-11.s.s2.fail.c3: The axis of symmetry is x=−b/(2a). Check whether this value is 2.
m-11.s.s2.explain: If the axis of symmetry is x=2, then −b/(2a)=2, so b=−4a, and if the y-intercept is 1, then c=1. Then a can be any value that is not 0, so for example x²−4x+1 and 2x²−8x+1 both meet the conditions. Since a is free, the equation is not determined.
m-11.s.s3.prompt: You want to get one more piece of information to add to "the y-intercept is 1 and the axis of symmetry is x=2" (option E) so that the equation is determined uniquely. What question would you ask the person who wrote the problem? Write the question and, in one or two sentences, why that information determines the equation.
m-11.s.s3.hint.0: Write which of a, b, and c option E has already determined and which you still don't know.
m-11.s.s3.hint.1: Think about what information you could substitute into the equation to determine a.
m-11.s.s3.placeholder: Example: Another point the graph passes through ...
m-11.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Does the information you chose determine the remaining unknown (a) uniquely?
m-11.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Is it information that does not overlap with the information you already have (the y-intercept and the axis of symmetry)?
m-11.s.s3.model.0: Ask for one point the graph passes through that is not at x=0 or x=4. The points at x=0 and x=4 are the same as what you already know, so they are not new information. Substituting one other point determines a uniquely.
m-11.s.s3.model.1: Ask what the minimum (or maximum) value is. The value at the axis of symmetry x=2 is the minimum, so f(2)=1−4a is determined and you can find a.
m-11.s.s3.model.2: Ask for the coefficient a of x². b and c are already determined, so if you know a, the equation is determined uniquely.

m-12.title: Looking at one arithmetic sequence problem
m-12.goal: Discover that in an arithmetic sequence, terms whose index numbers add up to the same sum have the same sum of terms, so that a problem that seems to lack information can be solved, and make a problem that uses this property yourself.
m-12.material: There is a problem: in an arithmetic sequence {aₙ}, when a₃ + a₇ = 20, find the value of a₅. Suyoung said, "We don't know the first term or the common difference, so we can't solve it." (Let the first term be a and the common difference be d. a₃ means the 3rd term, a₇ the 7th term, and a₅ the 5th term.)
m-12.thinking.0: Discovering a value that stays the same across many cases
m-12.thinking.1: Judging again whether the information is enough
m-12.thinking.2: Making a problem using a property
m-12.prereq.0: General term of an arithmetic sequence aₙ=a+(n−1)d
m-12.s.s1.prompt: Make three arithmetic sequences with different first terms a and common differences d that satisfy a₃+a₇=20.
m-12.s.s1.hint.0: Write a₃ and a₇ in terms of a and d, and write the equation you get by adding them.
m-12.s.s1.hint.1: Decide d first and find a from that equation.
m-12.s.s1.fail.c1: a₃+a₇ is not 20. Add a₃=a+2d and a₇=a+6d to check.
m-12.s.s1.explain: a₃+a₇=2a+8d=20, so a=10−4d. When d is 0, 1, 2, −1, the first terms are 10, 6, 2, 14.
m-12.s.s2.prompt: Find the 5th term a₅ for each sequence you just made. What do you notice?
m-12.s.s2.hint.0: Actually calculate a₅ for each sequence you just made. (a₅ is the first term plus the common difference how many times?)
m-12.s.s2.hint.1: Put the a₅ values you calculated side by side and compare them.
m-12.s.s2.o.a: a₅ is different for each sequence, so this information alone cannot determine a₅
m-12.s.s2.r.a: Check the values you calculated again. Think about how many times the common difference is added to the first term to get a₅.
m-12.s.s2.o.b: a₅ is the same value in every sequence, so this information alone determines a₅
m-12.s.s2.r.b: Even though the first term and common difference were different for each sequence, a₅ was the same for all of them. It could be solved even though the information seemed lacking.
m-12.s.s2.o.c: The bigger the common difference, the bigger a₅, so you need to know the common difference to determine a₅
m-12.s.s2.r.c: Actually calculate a₅ when the common difference is 0, 1, and 2 and check whether it changes. Notice that the first term changed too.
m-12.s.s2.o.d: The bigger the first term, the bigger a₅, so you need to know the first term to determine a₅
m-12.s.s2.r.d: Actually calculate a₅ when the first term is 10, 6, and 2. The common difference changed too.
m-12.s.s2.explain: For (10,0), a₅=10; for (6,1), 6+4=10; for (2,2), 2+8=10; for (14,−1), 14−4=10, so it is 10 every time. a₅ is the first term plus the common difference 4 times (a+4d), and from a₃+a₇=2a+8d=20 we get a+4d=10. Unlike what Suyoung said, a₅ is determined even if you don't know the first term and the common difference.
m-12.s.s3.prompt: Choose all the cases where, if you are told the value of the sum of two terms aₘ+aₙ like a₃+a₇, you can find a₅ without knowing the first term and the common difference. (You can find out by testing with the several sequences you made earlier.)
m-12.s.s3.hint.0: Write side by side the expression for a₅ in terms of a and d and the expression for each option's sum in terms of a and d, and compare them.
m-12.s.s3.hint.1: For an option whose sum is not equal to 2 times a₅, find yourself two sequences that give the same sum but different a₅ and check.
m-12.s.s3.r.a: a₂+a₉=2a+9d. The coefficient of d is different from 2a+8d, which is 2 times a₅, so you can't determine a₅.
m-12.s.s3.r.b: If you missed a₁+a₉: it is 2a+8d, which equals 2 times a₅.
m-12.s.s3.r.c: a₃+a₆=2a+7d has a different coefficient of d from 2a+8d, which is 2 times a₅. Look for whether there are sequences with the same value but a different a₅.
m-12.s.s3.r.d: a₆+a₈=2a+12d. The coefficient of d is different from 2a+8d, which is 2 times a₅.
m-12.s.s3.r.e: If you missed a₄+a₆: it is 2a+8d, which equals 2 times a₅.
m-12.s.s3.r.f: If you missed a₂+a₈: it is 2a+8d, which equals 2 times a₅.
m-12.s.s3.explain: aₘ+aₙ=2a+(m+n−2)d and 2a₅=2a+8d, so the sum equals 2a₅ only when m+n−2=8, that is, m+n=10. a₄+a₆, a₁+a₉, and a₂+a₈ all have index sums of 10. The others have different index sums, so the coefficient of d is different and a₅ is not determined.
m-12.s.s4.prompt: Using this property (if the index numbers add up to the same sum, the sums of the terms are the same), make an arithmetic sequence problem yourself whose answer is determined even though the first term and common difference are unknown, and write the answer and solution in one or two sentences.
m-12.s.s4.hint.0: Decide the index of the term you want to find and compare it with the indexes of the two terms you will give. Recall what you found in s3.
m-12.s.s4.hint.1: Pick one first term and one common difference, calculate by hand for the problem you made, and check that the answer is right.
m-12.s.s4.placeholder: Example: In an arithmetic sequence {a_n}, ... (You can type a₂ as a_2)
m-12.s.s4.selfAssess.0: In your problem, is the sum of the indexes of the two terms you give equal to 2 times the index of the term you want to find?
m-12.s.s4.selfAssess.1: Did you check the answer you wrote by picking one first term and common difference and calculating by hand?
m-12.s.s4.selfAssess.2: Does the solution make it clear that a friend can solve it even without knowing the first term and the common difference?
m-12.s.s4.model.0: In an arithmetic sequence {a_n}, when a_2 + a_10 = 36, find the value of a_6. Answer: 18. Since 2+10=12=6+6, a_2+a_10=2a_6.
m-12.s.s4.model.1: In an arithmetic sequence {a_n}, when a_1 + a_11 = 40, what is the value of a_6? The answer is 20. The sum of the indexes 1+11=12=6+6, so a_1+a_11=2a_6.
